content: Reading is the cognitive process of extracting meaning from written or printed text. It serves as a fundamental mechanism for language acquisition, communication, and the exchange of information and ideas. Proficient readers employ a variety of skills, including decoding (translating printed text into the sounds of language), utilizing morphemes, semantics, syntax, and contextual cues to interpret unfamiliar words. They also activate prior knowledge (as described by schema theory), apply comprehension strategies, and demonstrate fluency during the act of reading. Not all forms of reading are text-based; for example, reading can involve interpreting music notation or pictograms. In the field of computer science, reading is analogous to the retrieval of data from computer storage. Historically, reading printed text has not always been a primary means of accessing information for the general population. Prior to the Industrial Revolution, literacy was limited to a small percentage of people in many countries. Reading Skills and Development Various methods for teaching and learning to read have evolved, some of which have sparked debate. Phonics involves teaching reading by associating characters or groups of characters with their corresponding sounds. This method is sometimes seen as competing with whole language approaches. Whole language methods focus on acquiring words or phrases without emphasizing the individual characters or groups of characters that compose them. Critics argue that the whole language approach may hinder the ability to learn spelling effectively. Learning to read in a second language, particularly in adulthood, can differ significantly from learning to read a native language during childhood. There are documented cases of young children teaching themselves to read without formal instruction. For instance, Truman Capote reportedly taught himself to read and write by the age of five. Similarly, some individuals have taught themselves to read by comparing street signs or Biblical passages to spoken language. Notable examples include Abraham Lincoln and novelist Nicholas Delbanco, who taught himself to read at age six by studying a book about boats during a transatlantic crossing. Methods of Reading There are several types and methods of reading, each with varying speeds and purposes depending on the material and context: Subvocalized Reading: This method combines visual reading with the internal vocalization of words as if they were spoken. Advocates of speed reading argue that subvocalization can slow down reading and comprehension, though these claims are often based on controversial or unsupported scientific research. Speed Reading: This encompasses techniques aimed at increasing reading speed without significantly compromising comprehension or retention. It is closely related to speed learning. Proofreading: This involves reading with the specific goal of identifying typographical errors. Professional proofreaders often develop the ability to perform this task rapidly, sometimes suspending comprehension except when necessary to resolve ambiguities caused by suspected errors. Structure-Proposition-Evaluation (SPE) Method: Popularized by Mortimer Adler in How to Read a Book, this method is primarily used for non-fiction texts. It involves three stages: (1) analyzing the structure of the work, often represented as an outline; (2) identifying logical propositions and organizing them into chains of inference; and (3) evaluating the merits of the arguments and conclusions. This method requires withholding judgment until the work is fully understood. Survey-Question-Read-Recite-Review (SQ3R) Method: Commonly taught in schools, this method involves reading with the goal of being able to teach the material without relying on notes. It is particularly useful for instructors preparing lectures. Multiple Intelligences-Based Methods: These approaches leverage the reader's diverse cognitive abilities to enhance their understanding and appreciation of the text. For example, readers might consider hypothetical scenarios or predict how the text will unfold based on contextual clues. This can lead to a more vivid and memorable reading experience. Reading Assessment Reading rates vary depending on the purpose: Reading for memorization typically occurs at speeds below 100 words per minute (wpm). Reading for learning occurs at 100–200 wpm. Reading for comprehension occurs at 200–400 wpm. Skimming, which involves processing large amounts of text superficially, occurs at 400–700 wpm but often results in comprehension levels below 50%. Effective reading involves flexibility, adjusting speed based on the complexity and familiarity of the material. Speed reading courses often encourage readers to continually increase their speed, with comprehension tests suggesting constant improvement. However, competence in reading requires understanding that skimming should not become a default habit, as it can compromise comprehension. Types of Reading Tests Sight Word Reading: This involves reading words of increasing difficulty until the reader can no longer recognize or understand them. Difficulty is manipulated by using longer words, less common vocabulary, or more complex spelling-sound relationships. Nonword Reading: This involves reading lists of pronounceable nonsense words aloud. Difficulty increases with longer words or more complex spelling and sound sequences. Reading Comprehension: A passage is presented for the reader to read silently or aloud, followed by questions that test their understanding of the text. Reading Fluency: This measures the rate at which individuals can name words. Reading Accuracy: This assesses the ability to correctly identify words on a page. Some tests combine multiple components. For example, the Nelson-Denny Reading Test evaluates both reading speed and the ability to answer comprehension questions accurately. Effects of Reading Studies indicate that American children who learn to read by third grade are less likely to end up in prison, drop out of school, or engage in drug use. Adults who regularly read literature are nearly three times more likely to attend performing arts events, almost four times more likely to visit art museums, more than twice as likely to engage in volunteer or charity work, and over one-and-a-half times more likely to participate in sports. In the United States, literacy rates are more strongly correlated with weekly earnings than IQ. Reading books is widely regarded as a relaxing pastime that simultaneously stimulates the brain, potentially leading to at least a temporary enhancement of mental faculties. Lighting and Reading Reading requires more lighting than many other activities. Consequently, the comfort of reading in various settings, such as cafés, restaurants, buses, bus stops, or parks, depends significantly on the availability of adequate lighting and the time of day. Starting in the 1950s, many offices and classrooms were over-illuminated. Since the 1990s, there has been a shift toward creating reading environments with appropriate lighting levels, typically around 600 to 800 lux.
